s19 brings a lifetime (net present) cost result into a running-cost article, but it names the measure up front ('counting what the equipment costs as well as the fuel'), and s24 keeps it apart ('the studies that count equipment cost'), so it does not stand in for a running-cost finding. resolved.explanation: Deetjen's 'private economic loss' is a private net present value that counts the heat pump's net capital cost as well as energy cost (the paper's method, NPVprivate with Kheatpump). The sentence says only 'economic loss' and 'often economical', so in an article whose question is running cost a reader takes it as a heat pump costing more to run than oil. The assertion's qualification claims 's19 and s20 both name their measure as counting equipment cost'; s20 does not.
resolved.suggestion: Name the measure in the sentence, e.g. 'counting the cost of buying the heat pump over its life as well as the fuel, switching usually leaves an oil-heated homeowner worse off', so it reads as the lifetime-cost counterpart of s19 and not as a running-cost result.

resolved.explanation: 'Anyone switching from baseboards will see significant savings on their power bill' is the report's own inference from an energy figure ('up to 65 per cent less energy', quoted from Natural Resources Canada); it measured no bills. Repeated without that note, the article endorses a universal bill claim the package contradicts: Wilson finds only 73-86% of homes heating with electricity, oil or propane without AC would have positive bill savings, most of the rest in hotter climates. The closing clause ('compares heat pumps with baseboards only') limits the fuel, not the 'anyone'.
resolved.suggestion: Report the energy figure and say the bill saving is the report's inference from it, not a measurement, e.g. 'and infers from that significant savings on the power bill for those switching from baseboards'; drop 'anyone' or mark it as the report's word.
